title: Shared federal goals can create coordination energy without guaranteeing durable implementation
source_unit: GAO-26-108601 review of cross-agency priority goals and federal performance-management practice
geography: United States federal government; cross-agency priority goals addressing issues such as food safety, cybersecurity, and public-health preparedness

observations.period: Discussion groups and interviews May-June 2025; GAO report June 2026

denominator.unit: participant groups: former OMB political appointees and staff, former cross-agency priority-goal leaders, and outside performance-management specialists

framework.value: four-year outcome-oriented cross-agency priority goals provided a framework for shared federal performance issues

coordination_benefit.value: participants said the framework helped define ownership, created energy around shared priorities, and created opportunities for agencies to work together

implementation_gap.value: participants across all three groups said implementation could be strengthened

persistent_constraints.value: inconsistent progress tools, varying leadership engagement, and limited staff or funding to sustain efforts

recommended_controls.value: embed goal management in agencies, publish accurate progress data, plan for transitions, and strengthen resources and oversight
recommended_controls.unit: five broad approaches identified by discussion participants

observations.method: GAO review of statutory and OMB requirements, Performance.gov materials, prior work, and discussion groups and interviews with participants from three prior administrations and outside specialists.
observations.uncertainty: The report summarizes expert and practitioner views rather than measuring a representative agency sample or a causal effect of cross-agency goals. Recommendations are not ranked, and the report does not provide outcome estimates for a specific CAP goal.
observations.subgroup: Federal managers, former political and career officials, prior cross-agency goal leaders, and external performance specialists; agency experience and issue area differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared goals may still improve coordination even when outcomes are hard to measure. A leadership gap or inconsistent tool does not prove that an agency effort failed, and cross-agency work may require tradeoffs that a single performance number cannot capture.

related_sources.claim: The full GAO report provides the discussion-group context and five implementation approaches.

boundary: This record adds a qualitative cross-agency coordination and performance-management mechanism. It does not establish improved service outcomes, public trust, program effectiveness, or causal success of any specific cross-agency priority goal.
